summary:
Sucre is a department of Colombia and stands under Colombia's national framework. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier judicial route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside Colombia, and same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presentation of a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers.

The violence a trans visitor here is assessed against is national, because no Sucre-specific reporting was located in the sources reviewed. Hate crimes killed 13 trans people across Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. The case dominating that period is the killing of Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon, and no one had been arrested as of the report of 14 April 2025. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia.

Earlier figures follow the same line: 41 trans women were killed in Colombia in 2023 and a further eight between February and April 2024. Some of the targeting is organised and comes from armed groups. In Caquetá, the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes was given one week to leave town or be killed, and 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women circulated in the department. An activist quoted in the July 2024 investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases, so the charge available after a trans woman is killed here may not reflect the motive.

Access to premises and custody are governed by court order. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (guards at a Cali mall) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises, and a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, with a subsequent court ruling addressing the treatment of trans detainees.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's formal legal protections and the lethal violence recorded against trans people run alongside each other. The UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Organised campaigns have appeared in more than one department, so the Caquetá pattern is not confined to that department: in Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Flyer campaigns in Caquetá announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", and trans women in that department have few options beyond sex work.

The scale can be read against the first quarter of 2025: 13 trans people killed nationally in three months, against 41 trans women killed across the whole of 2023.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on identification through a notary by signing a document, a route available since June 2015, and identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers for people who choose them. Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition under Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993, with no surgical requirement.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. A 2011 ruling let a transgender woman prisoner choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a later court ruling addressed the treatment of trans detainees.

For residents whose partners were married abroad, the National Registry memo obliges notaries and registrars to register the marriage, after which healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights follow on the same terms as for heterosexual spouses.

The recording practice reported by an activist in July 2024 affects residents directly: the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and files such killings as ordinary cases, which shapes what investigation and charge families can expect after a killing.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Sucre-specific information was found in the sources reviewed; the department's profile rests on national figures and on campaigns documented in other Colombian departments. Whether armed groups have issued threats or kill lists within Sucre itself is unresolved.

The sources reviewed do not state whether the prosecutor's office handling cases in Sucre records transfemicide as a category, and the reported non-recognition comes from an activist quoted about Caquetá rather than from a published national policy document.

The comprehensive trans law reported as under legislative consideration in 2025 is not sourced here as to its current status or content.

Nothing in the sources addresses healthcare access, facilities or bathroom use, or policing practice specific to Sucre; the premises and custody protections cited are national Constitutional Court judgments.
